Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Baltimore MD/Washington DC
234 AM EDT Mon Aug 10 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Monitoring a decaying MCS this morning over western PA and another 
over the Ohio River Valley that brings the potential for severe 
weather this afternoon and evening.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) An active start to the new workweek with multiple chances for 
severe weather. Hot temperatures and high humidity continue.

- 2) Turning cooler toward the end of the week, although showers
  and thunderstorms remain possible at times.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1... An active start to the new workweek with multiple 
chances for severe weather. Hot temperatures and high humidity 
continue.

Shaping up to be a fairly active weather pattern today through 
Wednesday as multiple pieces of shortwave energy traverse the 
region. This morning we continue to monitor a decaying MCS as it 
moves across western PA, north-central WV, and toward far western MD 
early this morning. Most of the guidance dissipates this activity as 
it continues east with just a few residual showers and mid/high 
level clouds along the Alleghenies and north of the PA/MD line. 
Residual outflows from this system combined with an additional MCS 
back across the central Ohio River Valley this morning and a lee 
side trough will set the stage for thunderstorm development this 
afternoon and evening. Depending on how this MCS maintains itself 
across our forecast area today, or have its remnant outflow focus 
the development of new convection tomorrow afternoon. If the MCS 
were to totally fall apart before crossing the mountains, with no 
remnant cold pool making it further east, the development of 
thunderstorms across our area would be a bit more in question, given 
only weak large scale forcing for ascent and questions about 
where/if a lee trough would set up. 

What we do know is that whatever occurs the ingredients will be 
there for severe weather development. This is due largely in part to 
strong daytime heating with highs in the upper 80s and mid 90s. 
Dewpoints will remain in the upper 60s to mid 70s yielding heat 
index values around 100 degrees east of the Blue Ridge. The heat 
combined with a shortwave disturbance aloft should be the kicker for 
at least a few severe thunderstorms to develop. Current CAM guidance 
suggest a mash up between scattered clusters to a linear line of 
storms peeling off the Alleghenies between 1-9pm. Storms will 
initialize over the mountains between 2-4pm before advancing east 
into the metros between 4-8pm. SPC has expanded the Slight Risk 
(Level 2 out of 5) for locations along and north of I-66/US-50 with 
a Marginal Risk (Level 1 out of 5) across the rest of the region 
(outside of locations south of I-64). Damaging winds will be the 
primary threat with storms along with isolated large hail and 
isolated instances of flash flooding. Machine guidance continues to 
advertise a high ceiling on the severe threat with WxNext2 
probabilities of 45-70 percent and CSU probabilities of 15 to 30 
percent across the area this afternoon and evening. Damaging winds 
will be the primary threat with storms along with isolated large 
hail and isolated instances of flash flooding. 

Additional shortwave disturbances look to pass through Tuesday into 
Wednesday. Mid-level flow will increase during this time along with 
stronger height falls yielding more widespread convective chances. 
With that said, uncertainty remains in regards to timing, coverage, 
and location of the storms during the period. This is largely due in 
part to the evolution of any MCSs ejecting out of the Ohio River 
Valley/Great Lakes region along with the remnant outflows left 
behind. Right now, Tuesday appears to be the day with the greatest 
coverage of showers and thunderstorms along with an increased risk 
for severe weather. SPC maintains a Slight Risk (Level 2 out of 5) 
for eastern WV/far western MD and the Shenandoah Valley. A Marginal 
Risk (Level 1 out 5) has been outlooked elsewhere across the region 
for Tuesday into Tuesday night. Damaging winds will once again be 
the main threat along with isolated large hail and isolated 
instances of flash flooding. 

Beyond Tuesday, timing, coverage, and locations of storms remains 
uncertain despite strong mid level flow and increased height falls 
across the region. Shortwave disturbances will continue to pulse 
through although more cloud cover may be noted which could dampen 
the threat. SPC continues to highlight Wednesday into Wednesday 
night with 15 percent probs for severe weather. This aligns with 
machine learning probabilities of 10-30 percent probs across the 
area. These probabilities taper even more late week as the front 
finally drops into the region. Once again damaging winds will be the 
main threat with storms along with isolated instances of flash 
flooding. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Turning cooler toward the end of the week, although 
showers and thunderstorms remain possible at times.

Daily storm chances look to continue through at least Friday as a 
frontal system tracks toward the region. Ahead of that front will be 
several fast moving shortwave disturbances which will help aid in 
shower and thunderstorm development during the diurnal periods.

Th southward progress of the cold front becomes more uncertain for 
the end of the week, although it likely drifts south with time 
(especially Friday into Saturday). Both physics-based and AI 
guidance shows lower severe weather chances Thursday with declining 
instability. Showers and thunderstorms could remain possible though 
with the front nearby. For Friday and Saturday in particular, there 
may be a better chance of drying out as high pressure builds to the 
north. This will also bring a corresponding cool down in 
temperatures (potentially a bit below normal) along with lower 
humidity. The front won't be too far to the south however, and will 
likely attempt to lift north later this weekend or early next week 
as a low pressure system moves into the Great Lakes. Thus, some low 
end PoPs remain in the forecast each day through the end of the 
forecast period.

Temperatures will cool from the upper 80s and low 90s Thursday into 
the low to mid 80s Saturday. Overnight lows will fall back into the 
low to mid 60s with 50s over the mountains. 

&&

.AVIATION /06Z MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
VFR conditions look to prevail across the terminals through Friday 
given subtropical high pressure offshore and the lack of any 
significant front passing through. Brief periods of sub-VFR 
restrictions are likely during the afternoon and evening hours due 
to thunderstorms, especially today through Wednesday. Thunderstorm 
coverage lowers Thursday and Friday as a front gradually sags 
through the region. 

Storm coverage increases this afternoon and evening and again 
Tuesday as multiple shortwave disturbances pass through. The risk 
for severe weather is also increasing during this time with a focus 
during the peak heating period 18z-02z/2-9pm this afternoon and 
evening. Storms should initialize west of MRB between 16-19z/12-3pm 
before advancing into the corridor between 19-23z-3-7pm. Storm 
coverage remains uncertain with gusty winds, frequent lightning, and 
locally heavy rainfall as the primary concerns. Similar conditions 
are expected Tuesday and Wednesday with restrictions possible in the 
afternoon and evening due to thunderstorms. 

Outside of the thunderstorms expect patchy fog between the terminals 
each morning through Thursday. Winds will remain light out of the 
west and southwest at less than 15 kts. 

VFR conditions are expected this upcoming weekend with isolated 
showers and thunderstorms returning Sunday into early next week as 
the front tries to lift back into the region. 

&&

.MARINE...
A brief period of southerly channeling may return to the middle and 
open waters of the Chesapeake Bay this afternoon and evening with 
sub-SCA level winds over most of the waters. Overall sub-SCA level 
winds are expected through Wednesday. Wind speed and direction are a 
bit uncertain Thursday and Friday as a cold front gradually pushes 
through the area. While winds appear to be mostly sub-SCA at this 
time, there could be an enhanced northwesterly surge once the front 
does push through. 

Outside of the background winds, expect daily shower and 
thunderstorm chances are each afternoon and evening through upcoming 
workweek. Special Marine Warnings may be needed to encompass any 
stronger thunderstorms that may form especially today through 
Thursday. Damaging wind gusts and frequent cloud-to-ground lightning 
will be the main threats between 18z-01z/ 2-9pm.
